intro: Driving and delivery jobs cover a wide spectrum — from flexible local delivery and courier work you can do part-time, to full-time CDL truck driving that pays well and is in steady demand. Requirements vary a lot by role: local delivery usually needs a standard license and clean record, while commercial trucking requires a CDL. Some roles provide the vehicle, while gig-style delivery uses your own car. Because goods move everywhere, driving openings tend to be available in most areas year-round. Here's how the roles compare and where to find current openings.

bullets: CDL truck driver — regional and long-haul

sections.h: What the work is really like day-to-day
sections.p: The daily routine depends heavily on the role. Local delivery and courier drivers make many stops per shift, so the day is a mix of driving and getting in and out to hand off packages, which involves some lifting. Box-truck drivers handle larger loads and often help load and unload. CDL drivers spend long stretches on the road on regional or long-haul routes, following hours-of-service rules and managing their time carefully. Rideshare and on-demand work lets you choose when to drive, with earnings tied to how much you take on.

faqs.q: Do I need a CDL to drive for delivery?
faqs.a: No — most local delivery, courier, and box-truck roles use a standard driver's license. A CDL is required for larger commercial trucks, and some employers help you train for one.
Yes. Delivery, courier, and on-demand roles often let you choose part-time or flexible hours.

faqs.q: Which driving jobs pay the most?
faqs.a: Experienced CDL and long-haul trucking roles generally pay the most, followed by specialized box-truck and regional routes.

faqs.q: What do employers check before hiring?
faqs.a: Most driving roles require a valid license and a review of your driving record, plus a background check. CDL roles have additional requirements, and some include a road test or drug screening. Each posting lists the specifics.

faqs.q: Can I use my own car?
faqs.a: For gig-style and some courier roles, yes — you drive your own vehicle. Many local-delivery and box-truck roles provide a company vehicle instead. The posting will say which applies.
